Sheet 02.6 · datum A · locomotion mechanism

In preparation · second author

Testing the chain that drives and supports a stair-climbing wheel.

The pivoting triangular track wheel uses one printed chain for two jobs: transmitting torque and gripping the step. That makes the chain the main structural and traction risk. I joined the project as second author and started by designing a tensile test programme for the printed links.

My roleSecond author, experimental programme, and analysis
EvidenceTensile tests, costed BOM, material assignment, and scale study
Key pointThe chain and gear cluster dominate both mass and cost

Authors. Claudio Marzo · Revant Nitin Bhatt · Prof. Dr.-Ing. Ronny Hartanto · Prof. Dr.-Ing. Stéphane Danjou. Claudio Marzo developed the mechanism concept. As second author, I designed and interpreted the tensile tests, prepared the costed bill of materials, wrote the material assignment guideline, and completed the scaling study.

Where it sits

The paper organises the reviewed designs into four working categories: legged, articulated-wheel, leg–wheel hybrid, and tracked. Most stair-climbing concepts reviewed for this project separate power transmission from ground traction.

What the tensile tests found

Because the chain does both jobs, it carries the whole risk. I pulled printed links on a Shimadzu screw-driven machine and the load–extension curves fell into two repeatable families.

  • Family 1 - load collapses at peak and drops to near zero. A single dominant fracture, no load path left afterwards.
  • Family 2 - load degrades gradually and holds a clear residual. Something in the joint keeps carrying after first failure.
  • Grip orientation matters more than expected. Flipping the chain in the jaws changed the response markedly, which tells you load introduction is doing part of the work and the fixture is a confound, not a control.
  • Fracture is layer-stepped at the snap-fit corners. the failure follows the print layers rather than cutting across them. That's interlayer bonding, not bulk material strength, and it points at print orientation rather than material choice.

Where the machine's cost and mass live

Before optimising anything I costed and weighed the whole assembly at two scales. The result reorders where effort belongs.

Bill of materials. 100% scale wheel, polymer
GroupShare of costShare of mass
Chain links30.5%26.4%
Gear cluster incl. dog clutch52.6%57.2%
Frames, both sides16.9%16.4%
Whole wheel€ 108.424.99 kg

The frames. the parts that look structural. are under a fifth of both cost and mass. The chain and gear cluster together carry the overwhelming majority of each, which is where hardening effort belongs and why the tensile programme targeted the chain first.

Moving from 50% to 100% scale multiplied mass by 5.7 and cost by 5.6, not 8. Wall thicknesses were adjusted for printability instead of being scaled uniformly, so the result did not follow a simple cubic rule.

Scope

Completed: mechanism design, printing, tensile characterisation, bill of materials, material assignment, and scale analysis. Not yet measured: stair ascent, slip per step, and oscillation. The taxonomy discussion is based on kinematics rather than locomotion data, so the manuscript now leads with the design and test evidence and treats the taxonomy as discussion.
